newsitem.title: USA: White House to propose aid package for District.
newsitem.headline: White House to propose aid package for District.

text.p: The White House plans this week to propose a major aid package to help pull the national capital out of its deep financial crisis, a White House official said on Monday.

The package of initiatives, to be proposed on Thursday, calls for the federal government to help the District of Columbia pay medical bills for its poorest citizens, assume responsibility for a $4.4 billion pension liability and the city's prisons and courts.
In exchange for the federal aid, the District would give up an annual $660 million federal payment to offset revenue lost from tax-exempt federal properties, the official said.

If approved by Congress, the plan will result in a net cost to the federal government of $339 million over five years, the official said. It would spell savings of $770 million for the city over the same period, he said.
Under the plan, the government would pay 70 percent of the city's Medicaid bills instead of the current 50 percent, the official said, confirming a report by a source familiar with the plan.

In addition, the federal government would assume full payment of a massive unfunded pension liability for city firefighters, police, teachers and judges that the District inherited from the United States government when it won some autonomy from the federal government in 1974, the source said.

The liability had reached about $1.8 billion around 1980 and was now close to $4.4 billion, prompting Andrew Brimmer, chairman of the control board to warn that the pension problem would reach "catastrophic" proportions early next century.

The District of Columbia has been financially strapped for years, and late last year a financial control board created by Congress to oversee the city's finances ordered city officials to cut $85 million in projected overspending in 1997.

President Bill Clinton on Dec. 13 pledged a "systematic effort" to help the city, noting that its unusual status as a city without fiscal aid from a state had left it floundering in "a series of purgatories."
Hillary Rodham Clinton told the Washington Post on Saturday a series of concrete initiatives would be unveiled "in the next few weeks," although she provided few details.
The first lady has adopted the capital's cause, donating proceeds from the sale of her book to a children's hospital and participating in private efforts to help the city.

The White House also will recommend that the Justice Department take responsibility for the city's prisons and courts, including incarceration of the city's roughly 7,000 felony prisoners, the sources said.
The White House also will propose a package of grants and tax incentives aimed at encouraging business and jobs in the financially troubled city, the sources said.
The Internal Revenue Service would collect the city's annual income taxes, the White House official said.
Details of the plan will be contained in the FY'98 budget Clinton sends to Congress in February.

Congress must approve all the measures in the aid package, but House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich has taken an active role in improving the financial health of the city. The district had a $90 million budget shortfall in FY'96.
The control board last month asked the the federal government to spend up to $1 billion to help the city.
Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a deeply troubled city of 543,000 people, many poor and black.

The city has a high crime rate, but lacks fire trucks and other emergency vehicles; police cars go unrepaired and potholes are left unfilled. A former army general has been appointed to run its schools.
